summary_paragraph: An elderly male with a complex medical history including COPD, CAD s/p CABG, atrial fibrillation, cerebellar degeneration, and prior aspiration pneumonia was admitted for fever and abdominal pain localized to his G-tube site. He reported redness, pain, and drainage around the tube, along with recent cough and nausea. Initial evaluation revealed leukocytosis, hyponatremia, and a new lung opacity on chest X-ray, prompting concern for pneumonia and G-tube site cellulitis. He was started on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. CT abdomen showed no abscess but confirmed the G-tube in place and extensive diverticulosis. Over the hospital stay, his fever resolved, respiratory status remained stable, and the pneumonia concern was downgraded. He was transitioned to oral Bactrim for cellulitis. The patient expressed a clear desire to have his unused G-tube removed despite risks of aspiration, a decision supported by his healthcare proxy. He was discharged home with services on a 10-day antibiotic course with plans for outpatient G-tube removal, follow-up for iron deficiency anemia, and monitoring of chronic hyponatremia.
